title: Prediction Trust Ladder
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Trustworthy Prediction
Mastery Prediction
Evidence Standards
Learning Analytics
description: A Mermaid ladder of five evidence rungs for mastery-prediction claims (hoped for, designed, simulated, measured once, replicated and audited), joined by upward arrows. A click directive on every rung opens an infobox with the evidence the rung requires, an example claim from the book and what would move a claim up; a Place this claim menu offers six example claims and highlights the correct rung after the learner chooses one.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

educational.topic: How far a mastery-prediction claim can be trusted
learningObjectives: The learner will judge how far a given mastery-prediction claim can be trusted by locating it on a ladder of evidence.
prerequisites: Bias in prediction and ethical use (Chapter 24)

accessibility.notes: Each rung is a focusable button (Tab, Enter) with an aria-label; the infobox is an aria-live region; rungs on dark fills use white text above 5:1 contrast; placement feedback uses outline style (solid versus dashed) and words as well as color

controls.label: Five rungs
controls.purpose: Open the rung's requirements, example and next step; place the current claim

controls.label: Place this claim
controls.purpose: Choose one of six example claims to place on the ladder

simulation.model: Ordinal ladder of evidence for prediction claims (a planning aid, not a measured result)
assumptions: The book has no real-learner result, so the top two rungs have no example claim from the book
Two of the six example claims are hypothetical and labeled as such

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Judgment against an explicit evidence hierarchy with immediate explanatory feedback
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Clickable flowchart nodes with an infobox and a claim-placement quiz
keyQuestions: What evidence would this claim need to move up one rung?
Why is a synthetic result weaker than one real class?
Which rung produced the mastery number on a dashboard?
commonMisconceptions: A written model that runs is evidence that it predicts mastery
A good synthetic result transfers to real learners
One real class is enough to trust a prediction
assessmentOpportunities: Placing and justifying a claim from the learner's own work
